dataset.name: Storm and Annual Time Scale Hydrological Data for the Russian River Watershed 1996-2022
description: These files contains observed and simulated hydrological data (discharge, precipitation) that have been aggregated to the storm-event scale and to the annual time scale for the Russian River Watershed (RRW), California. Observed data are obtained from 12 different USGS hydrological stations located throughout the watershed, and discharge is simulated using the GR5H hourly hydrological model. Precipitation data are obtained from the NASA NLDAS NOAH Community Land Surface Model. All simulated and observed discharge are aggregated to the storm and annual time scales. We investigated changes in watershed hydrological conditions in the Russian River Watershed, a Mediterranean, drought prone, wildfire-adapted ecosystem, following eleven wildfires that occurred from 2017-2020. We ask two research questions: 1) How do interacting wildfire events, drought, and atmospheric rivers impact hydrological conditions of the watershed and in particular streamflow?, and 2) What percentage of new and/or cumulative wildfire disturbance is required to initiate hydrological change? We hypothesize that sub-watersheds of the RRW Mediterranean ecoregion have not burned beyond an intrinsic, and still unknown, threshold required to initiate change. Using a series of paired burned/unburned catchments nested within the larger watershed, we examined temporal and spatial patterns of pre-and-post wildfire water hydrology using a rainfall runoff hydrological model compared with data.

measurementTechnique:
The steps used to generate the data are outlined in the following publication:
Newcomer, M.E., J. Underwood, S. Murphy, C. Ulrich, T. Schram, S.R. Maples, J. Peña, E.R. Siirila-Woodburn, M. Trotta, J. Jasperse, D. Seymour, S.S. Hubbard. (2022). Prolonged Drought in a Mediterranean EcoRegion Suppresses Wildfire Impacts on Hydrology. (in prep for submission to WRR).
United States Geological Survey (USGS) National Water Information Systems (NWIS) streamgages were selected along the main stem and at the base of tributaries with a range of wildfire impacts to assess unique drainage area signatures that contribute to downstream conditions. Sites were selected based on the availability of hourly discharge data and records beginning at or before 2000. Larger stream orders were selected at the mouth of catchments to provide an aggregated signal from smaller sub-watershed contributions.

We used streamgage records from the 12 sub-watersheds across the RRW to assess the impact on postfire changes in streamflow and whether wildfire activity has detectable effects on streamflow. All hourly discharge data was obtained from the USGS NWIS portal using the R dataRetrieval package and converted to specific discharge (mm/hour) by dividing hourly discharge rate (m3/h) by the drainage area (km2). Precipitation, soil moisture, and evapotranspiration variables were spatially aggregated to each sub-watershed using Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) raster datasets.

Discharge was simulated for each of the 12 sub-watersheds for water years 2000-2022 using the R packages airGR which implements the GR5H hourly hydrological model. Calibration and validation was done using the particle swarm optimization technique for selecting parameters from the R hydroPSO package and vignette.

Using the observed and simulated discharge time series, we conducted baseflow separation during storm events to calculate two components of discharge: baseflow (undifferentiated groundwater and reservoir release contributions, m3/s) and quickflow (runoff contributions, m3/s) using the EcoHydRology R package.
